Author: @lumina1104
Content:
It's a bit biased to straight out call fentanyl "the most garbage drug." And potentially even intellectually dishonest. 

Fentanyl has legitimate uses in medicine. I was on 24-hour patches for 3 years. I recognize that there are places in the world that also use diacetylmorphine, the scientific name for heroin, in medicine. More medically approved opioids similar in strength to heroin, as opposed to fentanyl, exist, though. There are also stronger illicit opiates than fentanyl, such as carfentanil, an analogue of fentanyl, and nitazene. Since far fewer options similar in strength to fentanyl exist, it makes it easy to understand why having it as a legal option where quality control exists in manufacturing is important to ensure that the option is available for those in severe pain.  Since it has legitimate medical uses, and some stronger opioids exist, it makes it difficult to understand the selectively biased label of "the most garbage drug."

Author: @ErtugrulK
Content:
Heroin gave me wings, yet stole the sky.
It planted flowers in my lungs, but I was suffocating.
My blood boiled, while my veins burned.
I drifted into sleep, unaware it might be my last.

That night, one of the quietest deaths unfolded —
a death so silent, even I could not hear it.

I dreamt a dream, one I could never share.
And then, I was pulled back —
paramedics circling me like stars around a dying planet.
The pain of broken ribs from resuscitation
was lighter than the weight I carried in my chest.
Life returned to me, though I knew it would not keep me.

‘I watched my life unspool like a film reel.’

I tried to peel away the mask to speak my dream,
but a paramedic pressed my arm firmly against the stretcher.
Even Azrael, standing in the shadows beside the doctors,
failed to catch the trembling whisper of my voice.

This moment, this fragile now…
How had I arrived here?
My dream…
It only took a blink, a fainting,
and I fell back into it again.

‘What does it make you feel?’ I asked,
my voice laced with both curiosity and dread.
My dealer only smiled, replying:
‘It just makes you feel happy.’

That answer, so hollow and evasive,
blurred the line between this and any other poison,
and drew a furrow to my brow.

Naïve, unknowing,
I swallowed the small capsule wrapped in its film.
After all, how dangerous could a pill be?
How cruel could something so small truly become?

Haha…

On the bus ride home at dusk,
I could not tell what cut deeper into my ears —
the cries of a woman’s restless baby,
or the ceaseless noise of the crowd

This shows that heaven and hell are not external places, but rather human, spiritual constructs, reflections of our lived experience on Earth. Heaven is simply the feeling of joy and peace, while hell is the experience of pain and suffering. One cannot exist without the other. We often think we’re heading toward one or the other, but in truth, we need both to feel whole. It’s the healthy balance between light and dark, joy and sorrow, that creates true fulfillment.

The idea of a perfect heaven where we only feel good is a comforting illusion, but ultimately a misleading one. Likewise, the notion of a pure, eternal hell is an exaggerated fantasy. These are not truly separate realms, they are intertwined realities we already experience in this life. And as we can see through our own personal journeys, both extremes exist, just as much as the balanced middle does. We are meant to navigate them all, not to escape them.

Author: @glovere2
Content: I was on opiate pain meds for 10 years coping with a painful chronic illness. They enabled me to stay employed and functional but there’s always a price to pay with drugs like that. Last year I decided to get off of them in retirement and try to rebuild a different life free of opiate dependency. I never considered going back on them despite the extreme difficulty healing from so many years of dependence, which is totally different from addiction. Once I chose to get off them I never had an impulse to go back on them. I knew what I was in for and went for it and it was the right decision for me. Those drugs are extremely effective in certain cases when carefully monitored by certified pain specialists. I was able to make it to retirement instead of going on disability and having a very different kind of life. I have found other ways of coping with my pain and the downsides of opiate use are as profound as their benefits. That became clearer to me the longer I was off them. They are a godsend for those who need them and a wicked scourge for the addicted. It’s one thing to need a crutch when injury or illness breaks you and no other choices are available. That’s what they are for and there is nothing like them. It’s another thing to break yourself on purpose to escape emotional pain and end up in a far worse situation. For some people it’s a trap they fall into and cannot escape from through no fault of their own beyond the initial first use. It overpowers them and they are helpless to extricate themselves from their grip. They need support and treatment. I really feel for those in that nightmarish situation. What we need are advances in medicine and treatment for the afflicted. I have no doubt that future humans will look back at these blunt instruments as relicts of a barbaric past when far better and less harmful treatments are developed.

Author: @philoopnorth4901
Content:
I use legitimately prescribed fentanyl patches, created by properly controlled and inspected laboratories, and it still scares the crap out of me. The patches I use are supposed to release a controlled dose over the course of 3 days. Each patch contains multiple times a fatal dose for an opiate naïve person, and probably enough to finish me off as well. What if there was a mistake in production and the dose releases too quickly? What if I suddenly spike a fever while asleep and the dose releases too quickly? And, my biggest fear of all, what if I don't notice a patch has dropped off and some kid finds it? I use surgical tape to hold them in place, but I'm still paranoid about it. All that is with legit production and use, I can't comprehend anyone choosing to trust the scumbags that make and sell the illegal stuff (no moral judgement on users and addicts intended in saying that).

And, here's the thing, fentanyl is not even close to the scariest thing out there. There are chemical analogues of fentanyl that are much stronger. Fentanyl is reckoned to be about 50 times the strength of heroin, its analogue carfentanil is up to 50,000 times stronger. It's so incredibly strong that it's legitimate use is pretty much limited to stuff like tranquilising elephants. We know that illicit manufacturers like to mess about with the chemical formulae of drugs to try to dodge detection by chemical testing agents, so, there's always the chance of something even more terrifying being made.

Author: @seanswift8760
Content:
With over 40 years in the field of harm reduction — both professionally and through lived experience — I’ve seen firsthand what works and what doesn’t when it comes to responding to opioid use. What continues to frustrate me, and many others in this field, is the willful ignorance of proven international models that treat drug use as a health issue, not a criminal one.

Let me be clear: opioid dependence is treatable. People who use opioids deserve care, not condemnation. Yet in countries like Australia and the United States, we persist in clinging to outdated, punitive approaches that only exacerbate the very issues we claim to be addressing.

I’ve visited heroin-assisted treatment (HAT) programs in England and the Netherlands — programs that have existed for decades. These are highly structured, medically supervised services where people with long-term opioid dependence are prescribed pharmaceutical heroin (diamorphine) under safe conditions. I have witnessed individuals on these programs returning to work, reconnecting with family, and living with dignity and stability. The chaos, criminalization, and health harms that so often accompany street-based opioid use are virtually eliminated in these settings.

Contrast that with what we see in the U.S., where fentanyl is devastating communities. But fentanyl didn’t appear in a vacuum — it’s a direct consequence of prohibition. When governments crack down on less potent opioids like heroin, the drug supply shifts toward stronger, more potent substances. The War on Drugs, far from solving the problem, has made it more deadly.

Let’s call this what it is: a War on People. A war on people who use drugs. A war on people who are often already marginalized, whether through poverty, mental illness, trauma, or discrimination. Criminalizing these individuals does not save lives. It costs them.

If policymakers are serious about reducing opioid-related harm, they must look to the evidence. That means supporting safe supply initiatives, decriminalization, heroin prescribing programs, and wraparound healthcare and housing, not police crackdowns and moral panic.

The choice is clear. We can continue down the same failed road of punishment and prohibition, or we can follow the proven path of harm reduction, dignity, and care.

Author: @Hanszendent
Content:
How narratives about drugs awaken dangerous desires – and what they conceal.
Framing the first use of heroin as some kind of euphoric peak is not just misleading – it’s potentially harmful. 
What this narrative completely ignores is that people who respond strongly to heroin are often carrying deep psychological wounds – trauma, chronic emotional pain, a pervasive sense of inner emptiness. 
For them, the drug doesn’t produce a “high” in the traditional sense – it brings overwhelming relief. 

Not ecstasy, but silence.  - A break from hell. 

And that’s not something someone with a relatively healthy psyche is likely to experience. In fact, many report that their first use was underwhelming or unpleasant. 

So presenting this as a kind of ultimate one-time euphoria doesn’t warn vulnerable people – it entices them. 
It suggests there’s a magic moment waiting, if you're broken enough. 

Heroin replaces emotional regulation with chemical suppression. 
It freezes development, and cuts off the potential for healing. 

And what’s often left out: the people most vulnerable to heroin often don’t even know they’re in pain. Trauma doesn’t always come with a label – it shows up as emptiness, restlessness, lifelong tension. 
Heroin answers a question they’ve never been able to ask. But what starts as relief quickly becomes its own disease. 

Addiction isn’t just a consequence – it’s a predator. It changes who you are. 

It takes your agency, your honesty, your ability to love. You start doing things your sober self would find unthinkable. 
And once you cross that line, the addiction is no longer just masking your pain – it is your pain. 
Narratives that focus on the ‘one-time euphoria’ miss all of this. And in doing so, they risk making heroin look like a twisted kind of salvation to those who are hurting the most.

These oversimplified narratives may work for mass education, but when you talk to doctors and therapists who work with addiction every day, they’ll tell you: this kind of storytelling does more harm than good.

Author: @JanSheeesj
Content:
Hello, my name is Jan, and I would like to share my experience with heroin in the hope that maybe one person who reads this might think twice and to maybe add some things left  out by the video:

I am 24 now, and when I was 19, I tried heroin for the first time while visiting Los Angeles. There, I was introduced to heroin by some partygoers I met. After one of the parties, we walked through the city, and eventually, our group left the party to meet up with a dealer they knew. They seemed to have a very good relationship with him—both because his stuff was supposedly pure (he claimed 90–100% purity, though street heroin is almost never that pure, so I still doubt it was that high)—and the group seemed to trust him. They had known him for four years back then and always went to him for a dose.

We took the heroin, went to one of their apartments, and prepared the drug. I had never taken anything like that before, and they recommended I start with 5 mg of the pure stuff to get the best effect-to-risk ratio because my body wasn’t used to it. So we cooked the heroin, I injected it, and I truly felt like I was in heaven. My skin tingled, but pleasantly—like soft fur rubbing over it. Have you ever had a moment where you were really excited about something and felt a flutter in your stomach that made you feel incredibly good, like nothing could take that moment away? Imagine that, but with all the positive news in the world multiplied by 50. I didn’t even pay attention to my breathing because I didn’t care about anything else. (What i mean by that is that i didnt feel my chest rising, and I totally forgot i had lungs or even that I had to breathe.)

(According to the party guys I met) I fell back into the couch and just smiled at the ceiling with an open mouth and relaxed muscles. I had a broken finger at the time (broke it 2 weeks ago) and totally forgot the slight pain I had. In fact, I forgot I even had limbs. Imagine trying to feel what it would be like to control a third arm growing out of your back. You can’t. My entire body felt like this imaginary arm. Everything was just gone. The only things I felt were intense happiness, calmness, and my vision was blurry. Colors and sounds turned softer (after the heroin first hit)—like when you see a movie scene where a person is drowning, and from their point of view, every sound is dull and eventually vanishes entirely, with only blurry yellow and orange light remaining. My vision also didnt change much. It was like the things i saw at the moment of the injection were blurry and no matter what happened in front of me, all the silhouettes of the around 5 guys in the room remained almost the exact same.

At one point, I remember panicking for about two seconds (It felt like falling, but with higher gravity that made me fall a lot faster), and my body jerked (they told me after I 'woke up'). But I quickly returned to this amazing feeling. I stayed like that for about two hours in real life, but to me, it felt like just a few minutes—maybe 10. After I slowly regained control over my muscles and senses, I felt surprisingly bad and guilty. It was like everything amazing in life had vanished, like all the colors were gone, and there was nothing to look forward to. Similar to depression but not as extreme (I had depression earlier in life, so I think I can say that accurately). My guilt felt like when your parents or loved ones ask you for something simple, and you rudely decline, later feeling guilty for disappointing them and seing them cry later because of it—not an overwhelming feeling, but still rreally present. And like that I spent around 6 to 10 hours sitting on the sofa and just stared at the colorless objects and people around me. I did not have the slightest urge to drink or eat anything.

I also felt a lot of nausea and threw up three times that night (though I also drank about 7–10 cans of beer, so it could be because of that). My skin felt like it was drenched in fiberglass wool, especially my legs. I scratched myself so much that my legs were entirely red, and my left shoulder even started bleeding a bit. When I tried to stand up, I felt vertigo—not as bad as you might imagine, but it was still hard to focus my vision on details smaller than maybe a poker chip. Between 10 and 13 hours after the injection, the colors slowly came back, I felt happier, and I enjoyed spending the rest of the night dancing again—but not as much fun as before.

Overall, I would rate this experience as generally positive because I had so much more pleasure than displeasure. If every future dose were the same, I would inject heroin every day. But guys, it’s not like that. The happiness-to-displeasure ratio worsens with each dose. Many continue after the first dose because it still feels amazing for maybe 10 more times (I don’t know if that number is accurate). But after you cross the point where pleasure and displeasure are around the same, you just go down this hole. For me, it worked out fine because I only had one dose and had the discipline to resist the urge to do it again (it was a strong urge, like drinking water after running on a hot summer day—hard to resist but not impossible). But most will continue.

So in the end, I would recommend never even talking to someone who might introduce you to heroin. It’s a horrible drug, and before you know it, you’re basically in the middle of a deep addiction and almost dead. And if you really have to use any substances, I beg you, please choose something safer like weed or alcohol (safer, but still not safe. Stay away from that too).

Stay safe out there. Don’t do the shit I did. Please stay away from any kind of these substances unless advised by a medical professional.

Author: @Yusis-o7d
Content:
During last December I had to undergo intestinal surgery and was in an ungodly amount of pain, so the doctors administered smaller doses of morphine at points to alleviate some of it. 

It was one of the worst things I've ever experienced. 
I realized afterwards that I was laying on a medical stretcher and literally dying, yet I couldn't bring myself to care because the euphoric effects felt that amazing by comparison. 

My body doesn't really react to certain medications, and in some cases the effects are diminished. In the case of morphine I actually didn't receive any notable pain relief either, which made the experience even worse. 

I've since asked my doctors to always exclude opioids if possible, or to consider less intense versions, since the euphoria was that unpleasant for me. I can't even begin to imagine what Fentanyl would be like for me, and I'm perfectly content with never finding out.

The silver lining is that, from what I can tell, I'm not as easily susceptible to substance addictions due to how my body behaves, so hopefully I'll never have to find out either.

Content:
As a recovering addict who has done pretty much every opioid that exists?  I don't like fentanyl.  In fact most other addicts I know do not prefer it.  I MUCH PREFERRED HEROIN over fentanyl.  The high was better, it lasted longer, it had more euphoria, and the withdrawals weren't as long.  Fentanyl is extremely short acting, doesn't hit the mu-receptor as much as some other opioids like oxymorphone and hydromorphone, and while nods are usually the goal of opioids, fentanyl nods are usually just passing out.  There is very little euphoria IMO compared to other opioids.  I even preferred Vicodin to Fentanyl.  And, BTW, I had already tried fent BEFORE it became what it is today, back around 2010 before it replaced every drug ever because it's so cheap and easy to make.  Back when the only people making it where pharma companies who sold it in Actiq lollipops or gel patches that released micrograms over an entire day.  You used to rip open the patch and take the gel out of it and you could either eat it or try, and fail, to smoke it. 

So yeah.  Fent DOES "feel good" but not better than morphine in my opinion, and definitely not better than oxymorphone (Opana) or hydromorphone (Dilaudid).  THOSE WERE THE REAL KINGS of the opioids because they had better euphoria and, in the case of oxymorphone, wayyyyy better "legs."

Just my 2 cents as someone addicted since I got wisdom teeth pulled in 2008.

Also, despite it's EXTREMELY SHORT DURATION AND HALF LIFE?  Somehow the withdrawals from it are INSANE and not just the intensity.  THE LENGTH!  I mean everyone complains about getting off Suboxone?  I've done that successfully, MORE THAN ONCE.  Coming off fent was INSANELY HARD.  I have no idea how but fent would stay in my system OVER A WEEK (again despite its INSANELY SHORT HALF LIFE) and the withdrawals were just INSANE.  For not really a good trade off because it was so short acting a bag wouldn't even keep you well for a day.

I mean with heroin if you were broke and could only afford 1 bag?  Heroin has "legs" as they say that would probably get you through most of the day not being sick depending on how cut it was.  Fent?  Yeah you're doing the whole bundle you bought in 1-2 days because the effects just wear off so quickly its crazy.

Author: @occamsrazor1285
Content:
"So much lamer than heroin"...

Uh, as a recovering addict, I don't recommend that phrasing...

But this is pretty accurate. The problem is what I call the "rate of conversion", but to understand what that means, you need to understand the "wrath" of a drug. Alcohol will take its wrath out on you pretty quickly. It's called a hangover. this modulates use in most people. Alcoholics do exist, but it essentially takes effort to become one. That is to say, the rate of conversion to an alcohol addict is pretty low. Drugs like meth, cocaine and heroin (or other opiates) don't have a hangover. They require you to modulate use to prevent physical dependent. That's a dangerous predicament, and it's why so many "convert" into addicts.

Author: @route2070
Content:
Before getting started, I just wanted to share my experience. This is my medical fentanyl experience. In October, my colon ruptured, I thankfully had my phone on me. I called 911, and I was rushed to the hospital. They opened the ambulance door. My next memory was waking up 8 days later. During that period I had some weird dreams. In the following days, I also hallucinated. The hallucinations included included being in 8 different rooms, when in reality, I was in one. One of these days, I hallucinated being in the basement of a house, while still receiving treatment with a doctor, nurse, and Patient care tech checking on me. Later that day, I do remember being in a hospital room (at this point I am certain I was no longer in the ICU and instead I was in the cardio unit). That said, both in the "basement" and in the room, I couldn't finish a sentence. It was so bad tests were ran on me to verify that I didn't have a stroke, after those  came back negative, I had an MRI. Nothing abnormal, minus my missing colon. What preceeded all of this? I had surgery to remove my ruptured colon. My sedative? Propofol. My anesthesia? Fentanyl. I think they gave me too much, since the dosage of these drugs are usually based on weight, and I had an email (excessive fluid in tissue of 40-50 pounds (18-22 kg). After the surgery, they medically kept me asleep for a few more days to get me lose the excessive water weight, through dialysis and to raise my blood pressure (while asleep and on 4 pressures, my BP was 80/50). I am certain all the hallucinations, my brain fog, and my other issues was related to them giving me an excessive amount of propofol and fentanyl. That said. There was no time to make lose the water weight. If they didn't give me enough meds, I may have woken up mid surgery.  I feel like the way they did it saved my life. So while that week tucked, and now, nearly nine months later with wrist drop and foot drop issues still persistent, I feel like the doctors  did what needed to be done, considering the entirety of circumstances. 
Note, I am sure this wasn't me being high, but probably withdrawal. Nothing about this was pleasurable, I'm pretty I wasn't high when I was awake.

Content:
The information in this video about drugs is virtually true for all drugs. Taking a full dose of any drug for the first time will give you an absolute peak. If you keep taking it, you may come close to that peak a couple of times, but you will never reach it again. It won't be as good as it used to be, but it will still be "good enough." However, the longer you take the drug, the harder it is to reach the peak, while the other effects remain the same. This means that instead of being absent and happy, you will just be absent. If coming down was unpleasant the first time, it will still be unpleasant at any later time and will likely get worse. 

While other drugs may be less deadly, less harmful, less addictive, and less intense, what I said is essentially true of any other drug. I have experience with some of them. Not opioids or other extremely potent drugs, but even with less potent drugs, it's always the same story. At some point, you must make that choice, as discussed in the video. You either keep taking it forever or you stop taking it forever; there is no in-between. Even taking it "sometimes" means taking it forever. I'm glad I made the right choice and kissed all drugs goodbye at some point. This even included quitting smoking and drinking alcohol.

Author: @richardmark5427
Content:
I have a chronic disease that causes tremendous pain and agony, and during the over hyped opiate crisis that had nothing to do with medical patients who took it as prescribed, I was forced off all pain meds, so I, like so many others, turned to the streets, purchasing large amounts of 'blues', the things that used to be 30mg of oxycodone and were stamped with an M on one side and a 30 on the other scored side, which became mostly all fentanyl. 

Since there was no way the makers or those could properly dose them all equally with fentanyl, sometimes I'd take one and feel nothing, then other times I'd take  one and the next thing I'd know, I was waking up on the floor where I'd fallen suddenly and most likely very near lifelessly, had just slumped to the floor.

Seeing the obvious dangers, I started to powder all the blues, just so I could mix it all together so I knew it was all the same potency after I mixed them all up, and then just snorted a line when I needed pain relief, which probably saved my life, since it was truly only a matter of time before I took one that had a fatal amount of fentanyl in it.

Luckily, I eventually found a doctor who took compassion on me and •finally• gave me my meds back, thank God.

I haven't ever looked back and been forced to ever do any of that ridiculousness ever again.

I'm somehow alive today because society finally swung the pendulum back in the right direction and I'm not forced to use the streets to self medicate my constant pain, which ny the way is called the •most• painful chronic disease known to man, CRPS (or 'chronic regional pain syndrome'), and is often referred to as the 'suicide disease', due to the high numbers of patients who simply couldn't take any more of the ever worsening agony, ending their lives by their own hands, so I'm one of the lucky unlucky ones, I guess.

I'm just blessed that I got my meds back, or I'd be literally a 'ghost writer' right now.

The DEA has killed more of us innocent patients than anything else in this world has, and there's a VERY special place in hell for those responsible for sending suffering people like me to the streets, where many of us unfortunately didn't live to tell the hellacious tale.

Thankfully, I was never an out of control addict, and I only used them when I needed to, just like I responsibly took my prescribed meds when I had them, so I'm one of those who fentanyl •didn't• get, often called the 'minority', because I swear to God there were times I woke up sucking for air, I was so close to overdosing.

Society will look back one day on all this and know what a fools paradise they caused and how many lives were so needlessly lost by the DEA using their 'creative math' to lump all the illegal deaths in with the legal patients, making the crisis seem like it was caused by the very people like myself who never abused drugs, but were forced to face the decision to either find the relief ourselves, or take a bullet to the brain to stop it, which I damn near almost did many more times than I can count.

What a cluster£uck these times have been.

Sadder still, it was -ALL- guaranteedly intentional, as society considered all of us pain patients as 'unnecessary expendables' and they wanted us dead to unburden the system, so shame on them and I can't wait to watch them burn in hell for what all they put us through.

Author: @_____rnld
Content: Once I had access to a methadone pill (a friend - who is a physician - casually gave it to me). I kept it for a few months and eventually decided to try it out of curiosity while experiencing some mild to moderate pain. It was just one pill, and I felt quite good for about four hours. After that, I had a mild headache and a rather strong sense of sadness. I definitely felt it wasn't worth trying again. Nine years later, I was prescribed 30 mg morphine pills (every four hours - a pretty high dose) and took them for 2.5 days to deal with some acute pain. They did help - it completely eliminated the pain (good job, morphine!) - and I didn't feel high at all. But oh boy, after those days, I had so much trouble sleeping, going to the bathroom, and especially concentrating at work due to an intense feeling of unease! I even scheduled an appointment with a psychologist! After a week I was fine again. Next time I feel that kind of acute pain again (hopefully never), I'd rather take a lower dose of morphine and tolerate some mild pain to reduce the side effects. I can only imagine the unease and insomnia someone with fentanyl withdrawal must experience... Fentanyl is like 50-100 time stronger than morphine, and the withdrawal syndrome symptoms are probably much, much worse.

Author: @Professional-Gamer
Content:
I do fentanyl research and I have a few things I wanted to add.

1) I don’t really agree with calling fentanyl “garbage heroin”. It’s still medicine at the end of the day. I don’t want someone at the hospital being put on fentanyl then freaking out thinking it’s something that’s going to harm them. Fentanyl, in a controlled manner, is safe. There’s really no such thing as a bad or good drug in most cases. 

2) This would have made the video twice as long and is still new and complicating. So I’m a little happy it wasn’t brought up. But I wanted to add that fentanyl overdose isn’t the main issue anymore. It’s fentanyl + “something else”. That something else matters because it can really mess up the treatment and diagnosis side of things. Fentanyl alone can cause overdose; that hasn’t changed. It’s just fentanyl + xylazine, or fentanyl + nitazene, or fentanyl + caffeine, or fentanyl + anything other stimulant can have severely worse effects. Which takes it back to the issue about fentanyl being mixed in with other drugs by drug dealers who don’t care about quality control. 

3) Overdose rates have gone down amazingly the past couple of years. Most people believe it’s due to public awareness and naloxone distribution. The latest report showed we were around pre-COVID levels which is amazing. Everyone should have narcan (naloxone) at home. With that though, the Trump administration is trying to stop naloxone distribution. That tied to economic downturn is just going to cause us to undo the work we have produce. Please support naloxone distribution whenever you’re able to.

Content:
There are some people, including me, who've had to take codeine, morphine and fentanyl for severe pain and been legally prescribed it.

Strangely, I've never felt high from fentanyl  (I was on 100mcg patch for years but have succesfully reduced this now without issue) and only felt the relief and well being of having severe physical pain relieved. I've received higher doses than this via IV in Hosp though and never got addicted to it.

I can only assume then that these issues that were highlighted came from people either injecting fentanyl or taking tablets that were never prescribed, so they didn't know what dose they were taking which sounds extremely risky.

When you suffer from extreme physical pain due to a medical condition or injury I've often wondered whether the body reacts differently to it versus someone who's only intention is to get high from it.

However, I'd agree that tolerance to things like fentanyl can still occur irrespective of whether this is being used legitimately for extreme pain or used just to get high.

I'm fully aware that many homeless people use these types of drugs just to tolerate living on the streets and numb them from emotional trauma in life and I find that very tragic and sad.

Author: @MedorraBlue
Content:
I'm going through med school right now, and in my anesthesia rotation, I administered fentanyl a few times. Security on the stuff is tight, behind multiple locks and passcodes, and the dosing was very carefully controlled. (Honestly, my role as a student was more or less like being the person who clicks "upload" on an essay that somebody else wrote. Anyway...) What honestly shocked me was how such a small dose could put someone under. And I mean WAY under. So deep that even breathing stops. Obviously, it's all in a safe and controlled environment; but it freaks me out to know that such a tiny, *TINY* dose of dissolved powder could do THAT to a fully grown adult... just by giving them 1ml of it. 

Logically, I'd always know that the situation was perfectly safe... but every time I see it, I swear, it sets off some kind of ancient, primal fear in the back of my mind. Because if they fall asleep with their eyes open (pretty common), there is absolutely NOTHING going on behind their eyes. They're just... gone. And it looks almost exactly like death. Even though I know the situation is perfectly fine and under control, I can never shake that little voice telling me that there's something absolutely terrifying in that itty-bitty little vial....

Author: @jaylol7226
Content:
*Recreation*
To quote a friend who said this to me a long time ago: "Why do opioids when you can just do LSD?"

And you know, this much I can agree with. LSD will more than satisfy your curiosity if you're looking to get into drugs, not that I advocate that for just anybody, but you know who you are - the ones who have an insatiable curiosity and are bound to try something some time. I mean really, the choice is clear: Have a great feeling that lasts a few hours and come down into a hellish pit of despair and emotional wreckage, or have a great trip that lasts twice as long, has an extremely far higher required dose for lethality, and is far less likely to lead to addiction, unless you're psychologically prone to addiction. Not only that but LSD is going to make you realize things about your life that you probably never would have otherwise which leads to growth and change in a lot of cases. Plus, you get to see some cool pretty colors and stuff. Nice. Or, you know, you can conk out for like 6 hours and wake up having learned nothing and now your everything hurts for no reason. Why would you want that?

*Escapism*
Granted I am well aware that there are people out there who either are, will be, or used to be in a situation similar to my own 8 years ago, where addiction is a form of escapism from trauma, pain, etc. For me, that escape was in alcohol, because of the numbing effects across the board - emotional, physical, spiritual. I realize now that I not only made the issue worse but I completely barred myself from being able to heal from my pain.

To those people, I urge you: Do hallucinogens, NOT opioids (or alcohol or other drugs that will set your development into stasis or reverse your course of healing). There's a reason they're being clinically evaluated for trials in PTSD cases and other mental divergence studies: They actually bring something to the table. Nobody is out there doing studies on "the positive effects of alcohol in PTSD cases!" No. Don't do it! LSD or MDMA or similar, on the other hand? Yes. These drugs allow you to confront and DEAL WITH the issue in a structured way that will unstick your brain from the traumatic spot it's in and allow you to think about it from outside your trapped perspective, but you must do them with this goal in mind and a plan. They are not cures. They *can* help but it's not guaranteed. Alcohol on the other hand leaves you stranded right where your brain was at - it halts your development, it is not therapeutic in any sense of the word. Same goes for "hard" drugs like meth, heroin, fentanyl, downers like tranq, etc.

*Safety*
Do your research. DO. YOUR. RESEARCH. The Psychonaut wiki and similar sources are your FRIEND. They contain a WEALTH of information on drugs you've never even heard of, *especially when it comes to the actual dosages you need to take to receive desired effects.* Don't eyeball it. Don't wing it. Take it like it's a prescription because you're screwing with forces that human psychology/physiology wasn't really built to screw with. Don't trust ANYONE ELSE'S INFORMATION until you've cross-referenced it and double-checked it. Kurzgesagt has good information but you should remember that they boil things down and do not present it in an extensive form and there's a lot that must be left out for the sake of their short-form content.

One dose of methamphetamine can fry your axions in your brain, don't touch it. One dose of heroin can destroy your reward complex and is extremely difficult to escape once that happens. If somebody offers you something called "H", say no, that's just heroin that you smoke instead of inject. Don't even JOKE about taking Datura. Don't use diphenhydromine (Benadryl) more than a handful of times in your life - using it regularly even for allergies, even at a low dose, for around 3 years, that can increase your chance of dementia by 52%, and that's just an over-the-counter drug. You do NOT want to go to Auriel, you do NOT want to meet the Hatman. If you're considering putting ANYTHING in your body, make sure you're putting in only the requisite amount, and ONLY stuff that will actually give you some benefit!

2-CB (Nexus) is relatively safe at the usual doses (like, 15mg for a "standard" one if I remember right?). 4-AcO-DMT (psilocin - synthetic psylocibin) is safe, but pretty uncomfortable on the body, expect to be nauseous. Mushrooms are safe, but have plenty of side-effects, varies person to person and by the type of mushroom. They ARE toxic to you, do not ingest unwisely. MDMA is not safe but is a lot safer than a lot of things if taken at responsible doses, do not exceed 200mg as this just leads to diminishing returns anyway, anything more than this is pointless and just like other amphetamines will fry your axions if taken at a high dose or more often than once every 3 months at a standard dose. LSD is safe, but you'll build tolerance fast, don't use it more than a handful of times a year. You can get away with doing any of these without ruining your life. Consider the alternatives, people. It could save your life, and in a best-case scenario, even improve it if proper protocol, moderation, and a healthy dose of therapy are employed. You're worth saving.

Author: @Mickle-daPickl
Content:
As someone who hasn't ever seriously considered doing it, heroine has always scared me.

The fact that people who miraculously got clean from it and hate it to their very core, preaching anti-drug messages hoping no one falls into the trap they did, those same people, will tell you that doing heroin for the first time was the best experience of their life is genuinely one of the most gut-wrenchingly horrifying things I've ever heard.

You get the most bliss you are capable of feeling at all, you are in heaven, you touch God, and then you're sent back down to Earth within a few hours, and it's up to you what you do next. Do you live the rest of your life as a bland existence or do you use again? If you use again, eventually you start to use not to experience pure divine bliss, but to keep away anguish and torment from withdrawal. Your loved ones, home, job, education, car, and everything else is long gone by this point, assuming you miraculously aren't dead or jailed.

Just the fact that it's so good that nothing else ever feels that good, so you keep using until even heroin feels bland, but everything that isn't heroin feels horrible, and eventually you overdose and die is literally the scariest story I've ever heard, and it's the reality for so many people.

I wish this is how drugs were taught in school, because this is terrifying. I remember my school had a program called FOCUS, it stood for smth no idea what though, and all they did was just echo how bad drugs were, and that weed is a gateway drug. I literally though people ate drugs because they tasted good like candy, because the program didn't teach my elementary school mind what was making people use this stuff.

So basically, don't do drugs, heroin is scary, and we need to find a better way to teach that to kids, like this video maybe.

Author: @sweetboys2323
Content:
I was shy/bullied in my early years and drugs always held a lot of fascination as a way to change who I was and how I felt. I started smoking weed daily in college, then dabbled in other stuff. I was addicted to heroin in the 2016-2018 period. Just as fentanyl started to leak into the supply. I and people I used with would AVOID IT like the PLAGUE. Partially because of safety, sure, but admittedly I mostly did so because the high was nowhere close to H. You can use more and more H and get more and more warm euphoria... trying to climb to that 10/10 level high you got from your first use that you would unknowingly never reach again. But anything past a 5/10 level buzz for fent and you would just pass out or go unconscious. Fent knocks you out before you can climb too high with it, it leaves your brain instantly, and feels more numbing than warm. Fentanyl is more powerful for analgesia, which is why it is used in hospitals, but the ceiling for euphoria with any opium derived opiate like H/Oxy/Vicodin is sooo much higher.

Relapse has been a part of my story over the years and at times I have enjoyed 2+ years or so clean. The craving and urge to use always tells me that if I relapse I will get that 10/10 feeling again. But the thing people don't realize is that your brain adjusts to the drug permanently. My last relapse post 2022 I used a gram of H (I had to buy it for 3x the cost of what it used to be on the dark web... this seems to be the only way to get real H and not fent now), and got maybe 5/10 high for a few hours, then 3/10, and it NEVER let me climb above that. I used this one gram for 4 days while I was working a demanding job. Before work, once during lunch, and then right after. My pupils were pinned, but NOBODY could tell I was using because my brain is so permanently adjusted. I was not HIGH during this 4 days of smoking H, I just felt 'nice'. I just seemed a bit more social, energetic, warm. 

When I stopped, I had full on withdrawal symptoms similar to what I got after the first time I went to rehab. Back in the early days of addiction, I went to rehab for my first time after doing a gram a day of H for a month (this was an $80 a day habit), and had the same level of withdrawals then that I had on my recent relapse, using just one single gram over 4 days. The body never goes back to normal, really. The high is less of a high, the withdrawal is more painful. This same phenomenon occurs for alcoholics or even nicotine addicts and is called 'kindling'. There is a reason why it is so hard for a former cigarette smoker to have just one, their brain has learned how to rewire itself instantly in the presence of the familiar drug. 

That first 10/10 high I got, by the way? Was not H. It was vicodin. Two simple 10mg Norco pills. I used norcos a number of times before my H addicton, and NO other opiate... not snorting oxy, not smoking/shooting H, ever got me as high as those two norcos on my first go. With those two norcos I felt like I touched god, and initially months would pass between uses but each time I just "had to feel that release one more time", until I am where I am now. It really does feel like love and warmth in it's purest form. Not only do I have to carry that comparison with me in my day to day sober life, but I am physiologically locked from *ever* experiencing that high/love/warmth again. Even if I choose to use, it's not there. This is the DEFAULT experience for every addict. 

When I am sober for some time, I can be happy. I can form connections. I can enjoy hobbies. But there is always a boredom, an empty loneliness, a pervasive sense of thirst that even H itself cannot quench. Sometimes, I wonder if that's the missing piece that drove me to opiates or the missing piece that's a consequence of them.

Author: @armchaircommenter6805
Content:
Having received prescription Fentanyl for several months due to a major and life altering (but also life saving) medical procedure, I can absolutely confirm that Fentanyl is just the worst. I didn't perceive it as helpful or pleasurable in any way or at any point (although I can't really compare my experience to what it would have been like before), but withdrawal was still absolute Hell. The doctors told me to ease off it slowly once I didn't "need" it anymore, but after 2 minor dosage reductions I decided to quit "cold turkey" instead, because it would have just dragged out the misery endlessly and I wanted to get it over with ASAP. The doctors absolutely advised against that (probably due to the risk of suicidal ideation, especially in combination with the life altering part of the aforementioned procedure), but it was certainly the correct decision for me. Never going to allow Fentanyl in my body again, no matter what!

For comparison, I also received other opioids in the process and I believe that as an adolescent, I was inadvertently exposed to Heroin once (completely due to my own stupidity, not due to parental negligence or the like). The former was kinda good (but by no means just pleasure) and the latter was absolutely mind-blowingly amazing by comparison. Luckily I am a person that is not at all prone to substance addiction (rather, inexplicably almost weirdly immune, perhaps thanks to being a self-diagnosed high-functioning autist), so I still didn't have much of a desire to repeat the experience. I felt that it was kind of unnatural, too good to be true (or healthy) and therefore not worth pursuing. I guess I got really lucky for my mind to just work that way.

Author: @Beryllahawk
Content:
My one encounter with opioid was in hospital - I was given morphine right after a C-section. I don't remember much, morphine being kind of the littlest cousin in the family, but I do remember they told me I had only so much of it, and I could click a little button to get another little dose. "Dope on a rope" someone joked to me later. I was exhausted, so really all I did was sleep more soundly, from what my family tells me. The only thing I really remember, though, is when the limited supply ran out. I clicked the button, and nothing happened: and I immediately went "can I have more," even though by that point I wasn't in much pain and I wasn't as tired as I had been after the operation.
The amount I had was meant to last 24 hours, and was set up such that I couldn't actually make the button work until 4 hours had passed since the last click. Even so - in that short space of time, my brain and body WANTED it. I've heard people talk about morphine as a way to "make the world shut up for a while." There's an excellent and very upsetting novel written about a fellow and his struggle with morphine (Naked Lunch, don't read it if you don't want nightmares). But the primary thing I remember from that book was - the addict doesn't FEEL the needle. Or anything else. The morphine just "turns off" all the inputs, numbing existence to a point where you can think...and in some ways ALL you can do is think.
The effect is talked about in literature too, the idea of the Lotus Eater who pursues serenity to the point that they don't eat (and of course, they die); people used to rant about opium dens and how people would just sit and stare at nothing until they got kicked out for not being able to pay for more drug OR until they simply expired. And of course, the people willing to give other folks this kind of drug that is so dangerous and addictive - they don't care to regulate anything, they don't need to ensure their customers LIVE. There are a dozen more fools on every corner that can be baited, and a hundred dead addicts matters not at all.

Content:
As someone who dealt with heroine addiction years ago, I was hesitant to watch this video. Not surprising, it was quite hard to watch it at first, but finishing it was well worth it though. It reminded me of why I would never want to go back to that reality. I actually never heard of fentanyl until after I was roughly 2 years clean. A lot of friends I grew up with are not around anymore because of the opioid epidemic, and I personally don't think I'd be here if I kept using.

If you're addicted to heroin or opioids and want to stop, you can do it. It's not easy, and I highly discourage attempting it yourself. That being said, life will become a million times better than it is now, and is well worth it to get the help you need.

If you've never used an opioid, I would encourage you to keep it that way. You really don't want that in your life. It was very hard to break free from it, and even to this day, there are still dark parts of my mind that still think about it, and it's been over 10 years since I used heroin.

Source: I am an anesthesiologist.

Content:
Speaking of, the medical use for fentanyl is to treat severe acute pain. I received approx 200mg of liquid fentanyl intravenously last December to treat the pain from collistides, also gave me a cocktail of other drugs including anti-inflammatories. Barely took the edge off. Received the fent over a period of 4 hours, took 12 to stabilise me, and the fentanyl had worn off completely hours ago by then. Nurses lowered my dose, they were supposed to give me 300mg. (due to my weight)
All this to say it's a highly refined drug with one purpose: Very powerful but short term pain relief, and I mean short. Correct dose it might work for an hour or so, because it's only supposed to provide that relief long enough for other methods to be incorporated which funnily enough is usually more opioids.

May sound like a lot, but a) it was medical grade in solution, not pure. and b) I did not get even slightly high. When you're in as much pain as I was pretty nothing will cause euphoria, but fentanyl doesn't really get you high anyway.

Three vectors of neurochemical domination, each born from divergent yet convergent traditions of extraction, synthesis, and manipulation of the human nervous system. What follows is a breakdown of methodological essence, precursor logic, and transformational phases for each.

1. COCAINE: THE ALKALOID OF ASCENT

Origin: Erythroxylum coca leaf — ancient sacrament and modern stimulant. Process Archetype: Extraction, purification, and conversion.

⚙️ Phase Breakdown:

Harvest and Maceration: Coca leaves are soaked and crushed in a basic aqueous medium. Kerosene or gasoline introduced as a non-polar solvent captures alkaloids.
Alkaloid Liberation: Acid-base extraction yields crude cocaine base ("pasta").
Purification: Reaction with hydrochloric acid crystallizes the cocaine into its water-soluble salt form: cocaine hydrochloride.
Note: Essential reagents include lime (Ca(OH)₂), sulfuric acid, and ammonia.

Dopamine reuptake inhibitor — sympathetic nervous system hyperactivation. Euphoria. Vascular constriction. Addictive spiral via reward circuit overstimulation.

Origin: Fully synthetic — not derived from poppy, but from a phenethylpiperidine base scaffold. Potency: 50–100× morphine. Microgram-scale lethality.

⚙️ Synthetic Logic:

Core Scaffold: Aniline derivative → N-phenethyl-4-piperidone (NPP) as pivotal intermediate.
Amide Bond Formation: NPP reacts with a propionyl chloride (or similar) to yield fentanyl.
Routes Diversify: Analogues (e.g., carfentanil, acetylfentanyl) emerge from minor substitutions — methylation, halogenation, etc.

NPP and 4-ANPP: Heavily monitored pre-precursors.
Fentanyl’s power lies in minimal mass, maximal effect.

μ-opioid receptor agonist. Sedation, euphoria, respiratory depression. Death often results from unnoticed hypoxia — the “peaceful suffocation.”

Origin: Petrochemical — no plant basis. Derivative of phenyl-2-propanone (P2P) or pseudoephedrine. Synthesis Trees: Two major roots:

⚙️ (A) Pseudoephedrine Route (Reductive Pathway):

Reduction: Pseudoephedrine → meth via red phosphorus + hydroiodic acid (HI)

Strong odors: ammonia, solvents (ether, toluene, acetone).
Waste: reactive metal residues, acidic/caustic byproducts.
🧠 Impact Profile:

Dopaminergic and noradrenergic overstimulation. Euphoria, hyperfocus, aggression. Long-term neurotoxicity — dopamine neuron attrition, psychosis.

Author: @WinstonGuitar
Content:
Most people don't understand the direct mechanism by which drugs cause your death. Cocaine kills you by creating cardiac arrhythmias, literally causing your heart to misfire and not properly pump blood. Heroin kills you by decreasing body temperature, heart rate, breathing, and neurological activity. Alcohol kills you by slowly damaging your liver until it can no longer purify your blood. In reality, most drug deaths are caused by mixing various drugs into a rapidly-deadly combination, combining heroin+cocaine, alcohol + a "downer" of some sort.
But fentanyl kills you very rapidly by stopping your breathing. This fact is not well-known and is under-reported, and soft-pedaled by people who know better. A single dose of fentanyl can kill you. If that dose is more potent than you were told, if your body weight is less than what your idiot drug dealer thought it was, if you have an entirely empty stomach, or if, for some reason, your metabolism or reactivity to the drug is heightened. And you'll discover this fact, not by a near-miss, not by waking up a few hours later, saying "Bummer, dude! I'd better be more careful." You'll discover this fact by dying because you stopped breathing. Someone will find you dead. I'm not sure why educators muddle this fact with all kinds of irrelevant precursors. Fentanyl is not like other drugs. It will directly, quickly stop you from breathing.

Content: I've got a slightly different addiction than opioids, but it is one that you should know nevertheless, especially because it's legal to possess and purchase, and often strongly encouraged by society. THC addiction is something that, for over a decade of my youth, I wrote off as unrealistic. That all changed in my early 20s when I couldn't get regular marijuana anymore (my friend went to prison), so I decided to go to the vape shop and try a delta 8 THC cart. The first hit made me cough worse than I ever thought I could, but then the familiar bliss crept through my mind, just as strong as before. I decided that this was worth the cough, and as a plus, I could do it almost wherever and whenever I wanted now. No smell, no pipes or papers that took up space and smelled by themselves, I could just stick the vape in my pocket and be high all the time. And I was. For over two years, I've been getting high from the moment I woke up to the moment I fell asleep. I learned quickly how to be functional while high, and within the first week, I could pass for sober doing just about anything. One day, I was in a situation where the vape ran dry, and I couldn't afford more. That day, I was a completely different person. The rage was immeasurable, and nothing mattered to me. It was hard. Hard to look at myself, hard to be myself, then I got a vape again, and it immediately felt like I could enjoy things again. Delta 8 THC will go down as probably one of the worst decisions I've made. My mental clarity is way down. My brain is foggy all the time now, even when I don't vape at all. The withdrawal from Delta 8 doesn't have many physical symptoms for me, but it takes my mind to another place altogether. I caution anyone and everyone against using marijuana of any kind on a regular reoccurring basis. Every now again is probably fine, but never, and I mean never touch Delta 8.

Content: Pretty good overview, but you miss the fact that actually you can live a pretty okay life ifyou take a steady dose of an opioid like the situation where you get prescribed opioids from a doctor in a harm reduction strategy. Author: @gavinmagill5184
Content:
This video just mirrors the racist arguments that crack is "garbage cocaine" or that methamphetamine is "garbage adderall". Fentanyl isn't "garbage heroin", the main differences between the two are duration and potency (meaning it takes less fentanyl to get a similar level of high as heroin). With this in mind, the argument ultimately boils down to "poor people who can only get fentanyl/meth/crack are garbage compared to rich people who can use heroin/adderall/cocaine". 

If you used pure fentanyl (or heroin) once at a normal dose, it would certainly feel blissful, but not at all like the best thing you can imagine (I'm personally not a massive fan despite the euphoria), nor would you be craving more immediately (if you've been on twilight anesthesia, it's probably a combination of fentanyl + a benzodiazepine). 

It brings up CDC fentanyl overdose data to argue that it's inherently more dangerous to take fentanyl than heroin, and has a whole section on fentanyl being the perfect drug for dealers despite users not seeking it out, yet it doesn't talk about the drug policies that prevent those users from getting the safer drugs they actually want, nor the fact they're receiving completely unknown quantities. 

In fact, if you look at the CDC's own data on "opioid successes" for reducing prescription rates across several states and compare it to their overdose rates, you can see that overdose rates actually go up as prescription rates go down.

Unfortunately, the war on drugs has shown us that fear-mongering like this video is ineffective and just contributes to misinformation. I've had people tell me they're scared to carry Narcan because they still believe the myth that you can absorb fentanyl through the skin and overdose.

There's only one way to truly ease this, you have to quit and go through both the acute and post acute withdrawal stages, these can last a very long time for some, however, continuation only ensures more suffering later. 3:  Everything becomes less enjoyable during withdrawal: Music, coffee, video games, playing instruments, conversations, spending time with loved ones, everything that was once enjoyed will feel less enjoyable and perhaps not even enjoyable at all. It's not worth it, and it causes more suffering than anything else, it's a trap that seems appealing at first glance, but it really isn't trust me. 

Also forgot to mention: Some people stop caring about personal hygiene along with the things they absolutely need to do to ensure their survival and quality of life. This occurs because the drug in question and the feeling it provides becomes the most important thing to you once you become addicted to it. This is very pronounced with certain drugs, and can occur rather quickly, while it comes on somewhat slower for others. The false sense of security drugs provide can also make you do things you would never do otherwise, this can be quite dangerous, as you might feel more confident, but you aren't in any less danger.

Author: @yvindlind3223
Content:
This was a disappointing video from the @kurzgesagt team. What could have been a rather useful and concise video about fentanyl, which truly is a garbage drug, turned into a rote repetition of the same opiate fearmongering that used to be the standard several decades ago.  Even when the science has advanced. Even when you yourselves posted an up to date video on the nature of the drug industry and addiction, but then chose to delete the WHOLE VIDEO just because the "rat park" experiment results could not be reliably reproduced.

The simple fact is that several opioids have an "addiction potential" resembling that of alcohol when taken orally. This potential increases with snorting, then smoking, and finally injecting. So, the overwhelming majority of people who use opioids recreationally, do not become addicted. The number of people addicted becomes even smaller when you factor in the medical use, even when a large amount of patients  use enough to have to contend with withdrawal.

The really sad aspect of this video is how it contributes to the stigma against those who need it the least: the opioid addicts. In stead of articulating the myriad nuances around what makes an addict, you revert back to the outdated and cliche notion of reducing an addict to the moment the chose to try an opioid. Making it look like a mater of having such a low inclination toward responsibility and character that one would willingly step into a supernova of pleasure the moment before it turns into a black hole of eternal pain. 

This isn't helpful for opioid addicts, isn't helpful for anyone vulnerable to opioid addiction or addiction in general, and it sure as hell isn't helpful for those of us who are working to support relatives or friends who struggle with opioid addiction.

I strongly suspect that you guys know better, but still choose the most normatively vanilla perspective you could take on this complex issue in order to garner the most views possible. In doing so you are throwing the actual opiate addicts under the bus. Shame on you.

Author: @Ziorac
Content:
When I had a herniated disc, my GP gave me tramadol for the pain. A type of opiod. It did nothing for the pain and didn't make me feel anything euphoric, but the doctor told me I had to let it build up in my system for it to work. Okay, fine. A few moths later, I'd forgotten to renew my dose, so I was doing 100mg instead of 400mg a day. And I started feeling more depressed and anxious and stressed, but I have those things anyway, so I figured I was just going through a dip, keep on carrying on. Then a few days after that, I started to feel nauseous and dizzy. And that's not normal. And I thought 'wait a minute. I know these symptoms. I'm going through fricking withdrawal?! I was addicted to this piece of shit??' Needless to say I was very upset. I called my dad to get my prescription, cause I needed it now.  
Talked to my GP, said I'd stay on it till after my surgery and then we'd slowly lower the dose. Took me 4 months to quit. 

The worst part is, after the surgery while I was still addicted to the tramadol, guess what the surgeon gave me? Oxycodin. More opiods. I threw that shit away the second I got home. I wasn't gonna get hooked on two of those. Crazy how easy they give that shit out.

Author: @TomShlorp
Content:
This video is *excellent* ! This is exactly the true, honest talk I wish we were having with regards to drugs in our societies!

Edit: it also shows the effects of the war on drugs and prohibition. No one wants this, yet it’s everywhere. Designer drugs (“bath salts”) are another example. The demand is there, if the supply side stays being a black market environment, then it *will* follow black market rules: the most successful actors are the best at being criminals; and the people “best at being criminals” are the most violent, unscrupulous, greedy and ruthless - cartels, mafias, sociopaths and gangs.
There is no magic fix & it will *forever* be a problem (unless we find a medical solution to addiction and binging), but I am very sure there are ways to make it *better* than how it is currently being handled. Cannabis is a great example; the “backwards” US that many Europeans laugh at are leading in cannabis politics; yet in my country (Germany) right-wing politicians, the police unions and DAs (who would have guessed /s) want to get cannabis criminalized again - after just 1 year of a half-hearted, weakly implemented (read: bound to fail) legalization. Walking in circles here; there’s a reason the “German Michel” is a century old meme…
It’s all emotions, all ideology and zero will to find better ways than the current “adding insult to injury” approach, with having not only drugs ruin people’s lives but also adding “governments ruining peoples lives” (prison, trials, house searches, detention, criminal record, loss of job, social ostracism etc.) to it.
I am sure drug politics will be an area where our grand-children will look back and be embarrassed about how big of a moron we were, just as we look back to the witch trials…

Author: @mach2223
Content:
Just a big important thing I feel people should know: Weed does NOT contain fentanyl. Ever. The reason is 2 fold: Fent is way more expensive than weed, so putting it into weed is really not very useful for anyone.

The second reason is that cannabis combusts at around 600-900°C, way too hot for fentanyl to actually evaporate and end up in your lungs without being destroyed. So if you're at all worried about it, opt for a traditional smoke rather than vaping, which could make any trace fentanyl evaporate and end up in your lungs, or making edibles, which really is just a quick pathway into your bloodstream via your stomach.

But again, the actual risk of it being there in the first place is miniscule. No one's adding it on purpose, and the only way it could get there is through accidental exposure to trace amounts by large smugglers who were handling both in the same space. These smugglers don't even bother with weed anymore, since the price to weight ratio is way lower than synthetic drugs like fent or meth, and the rapid spread of home growing equipment and seed availability have significantly improved both the availability and quality of cannabis compared to smuggled brick weed of the 70s and 80s, therefore making smuggling weed really not a worthwhile effort to anyone when compared to locally grown product.

Author: @DyingToLive310
Content: This was my experience but with vicodin. I have Crohns Disease and needed pain killers for flare ups. Problem was I got reliant on it. I've always been a miserable, hate people, hate society kind of person. I never felt normal. I didn't like playing with other kids. I just liked beint in my room and reading books about any other life than mine. The medication changed me, it had the polar opposite effect on me. It didn't make me drowsy and zombie like. It made energetic and happy. I stopped getting that feeling after a few years and the pain wasn't going away. For a month I got switched to oxy and that's where I realized I had a problem. I would run out quickly and needee more. I knew if I ever touched heroin I'd be hooked for life. So I tried quitting. My pain was so severe and my mental state even after a year was bad enough id rather die from an OD than be off pain meds. But they were ruining my life. From 17-26 my life was tied to how many pills I had left and when I run out what will I do. I hated existing. Luckily I shopped to the right doctor after relapsing. He told me to get off it and prescribed me subutex. I felt no high, no withdrawals, no side effects. It got rid of the pain for 12 hours and fixed the pleasure side of my brain that's been broken my whole life. I go to hospitals and tell them no pain killers. I was handing my wife oxy after her pregnancy due to her surgery and never even thought about taking one. I have kids, a good job and I'm happy. A normal... natural happy. I've been on it for 8 years since it's not being prescribed to me as a drug treatment medicine, it acts as my pain medication. And after 8 years the pain still goes away. No tolerance build up. This medication saved my life. Yes very addiction behavior to say I like who I am on my meds. But the person I was hated life due to the pain. If you're like me and you need something to get you off the path of death, but you can't quit due to health problems. Ask about treatment. I'm glad I did. My Crohns doesn't control my life anymore. And neither does my addiction. I wish it was more well known. Subutex is the reason I'm alive today.

Author: @PetrifiedNightmares
Content:
I'm a psychopharmacology nerd and here I'll explain exactly how and why fentanyl is so deadly and such a low quality opioid compared to others. I'll then discuss the endless possibilities for incredibly safe alternatives in new drug discovery in this space. 

Warning though, it's long: Read on if you're curious and got a bit of time:

The Mu-Opioid Receptor is a G-Protein Coupled Receptor (GPCR) and has numerous pathways that can be activated depending on how and where a chemical binds to the receptor. Based on our findings, the G-Protein cAMP pathway is responsible for most of the desired effects of opioids: euphoria, anxiety relief, pain relief, resilience, muscle relaxation, sedation. 

On the other hand, the beta-arrestin2 pathway has been found to be responsible for almost all of the negative side-effects associated with opioids: respiratory depression (this is what kills you in an overdose, you stop breathing), suppression of air hunger (so you dont even notice that you're running out of air), constipation, rapid tolerance increase, rapid dependence increase and hellish withdrawals.

From this, it becomes clear that Opioids that favor the cAMP pathway over the beta-arrestin2 pathway are superior. Using morphine as a standard, some examples of safe opioids are: O-DSMT which only has 28% of the beta-arrestin activation of morphine (for an equivalent level of cAMP activation), buprenorphine (I don't remember the stats off the top of my head), 7-OH-mitragynine and Mitragynine, which has 0% of the beta-arrestin activation of morphine. These opioids are well known to be way safer in an overdose (requiring absurd amounts thousands of times higher than a standard dose to kill), have fewer side effects, and takes longer to get hooked to. But they still aren't perfectly safe, for various reasons. 

Oxycodone, for comparison is about 98% of the beta-arrestin activation as Morphine, effectively being of similar side-effect profile.

Now let's look at fentanyl. For an equivalent level of cAMP activation as morphine, fentanyl activates the beta-arrestin2 pathways a whopping 220% more! 

This fact, combined with its extreme potency (the stuff is active in the micrograms, which are literally microscopic specks), makes it very clear why fentanyl has such a bad track record. Users of fentanyl also often complain that it is far less euphoric than heroin and other opioids that were available in the past. And this fact explains why. Due to activating the dangerous pathway 2.2x more than a comparable dose of morphine, you basically can't push the limits with fentanyl at all without risking death. Whereas with other opioids you can take much higher doses before anything dangerous happens, allowing for a ton more euphoria. 

Another way of looking at it is that, fentanyl has 2.2x less cAMP activation per equivalent beta-arrestin activation as morphine, and thus it makes sense for it to be roughly 2x less euphoric.

So the extreme beta-arrestin2 activation explains why fentanyl has such a small therapeutic window (the ratio between a deadly dose and a standard dose). And because it is so potent, it is very difficult to avoid minor mistakes in dosage. And with such a strong beta-arrestin activation, and such high potency, even tiny mistakes could quickly become deadly.

Fentanyl really is one of the worst opioids out there. It is deadly, more addicting, has more side effects, difficult to dose, and barely even does its primary job (pain relief and euphoria) in the first place due to having such low cAMP activation! 

I'm very excited about psychopharmacological research into more g-protein biased MOR agonists (opioids). We are finding numerous interesting ones with various cool effects, such as SR-17018, which is a really cool new discovery that has been helping loads of people safely quit more dangerous opioid habits. SR-17018 is a strongly g-protein biased opioid that can completely cancel the withdrawals experienced from trying to quit fentanyl for example. However, it activates the g-protein pathway in a special way (that we don't fully understand yet based on the latest papers I've read) such that it doesn't actually produce much of a psychotropic effect. It takes the dope sick away, helping to stop you from reaching for another hit, while at the same time not making you high, so you can mentally move on from chasing the rush. 

GPCRs are really fascinating precisely because they allow for numerous different conformations that allow for countless possible pathways. I'm super excited to see what new discoveries are made in this field, and what more fascinating behaviors we can squeeze out of the mu-opioid receptor by activating it in just the right ways. 

Perhaps one day we will discover the holy grail of pain treatment: an opioid as effective and euphoric as heroin, but with as low of an OD risk as weed, and also carries 0 physical addiction, nor any increased psychological addiction (beyond you simply enjoying it, which activates the deltaFosB addiction/habit pathways all the same as a drug induced addiction), and never builds up a tolerance. 

The possibilities are endless, and I'm super excited to see what amazing discoveries we find out next about our brains.

This promotes an ignorant myth:  The reality is Fentanyl doesn't actually feel all that great.  It's a dull unfulfilling and short-lived high, compared to say, heroin. Fentanyl just gets its reputation from the dose required for subjective effects to begin being much less by weight... but there is a small window for when these starts, and when these get dangerous... what the "weight" or "mg" of the dose, is largely irrelevant to the end user, and only matters to the distributors... you can't safely "take more" fentanyl by weight "to get even higher" than traditional opiates, you'd just die....  And its characteristics are nowhere near as euphoric or long-lasting as traditional opiates within the window you can safely take.  People chase fentanyl much more like a crack addict chases crack, because of how much "weaker" it actually subjectively is, in all ways, in any safe dose, by its end users.    It's messed up.  If you can't tell, everything about Fentanyl is a drug dealer's dream, and makes for an even more awful and desperate reality for end users....

Subjective effects by end users though, heroin is much more pronounced in euphoria, and lasts a great  deal longer than fentanyl.  So basically, at a typical recreational dose by  an end user, the subjective effects of heroin are stronger, longer lasting, and more pronounced in all the qualities one has historically sought from opiates.  The whole idea that "fentanyl is 100x stronger than heroin" pushed by the media, couldn't possibly be more ignorant, and does not actually  accurately reflect  the subjective realities of end users, and what a "safe dose" actually looks like on either drug. Author: @MurakumoVance
Content:
I love how this video told me a lot about myself even though it covered vastly different subject matter.
I have Type 1 Autism, and by far the most successful drug I've ever taken has been "Adderall."  And I eventually found out that Adderall is just a cousin to Heroine.
Funny enough, Adderall just feels like a placebo to me...  Like, I really can't feel it working. I don't feel much of a difference at all. 
But I think it's worth mentioning that I have a ridiculously high pain threshold. And I know this because I developed an abscessed tooth in late 2009 that haunted me for over a decade. That thing went septic TWICE. And for anyone who doesn't know what that means, it's basically when the infection digs itself so deep into you, that it circulates through your bloodstream. Doctors stated that I was lucky to be alive. And a lot of people are amazed that I didn't suffer permanent brain damage during either assaults on my nervous system.

I find my neurological pathways to be fascinating on its own, because I ABSOLUTELY cannot relate to "addiction." Even when hit with addicting things, I find it unappealing. I was once addicted to Hydrocodones, and stepped up to Morphine. But I was only addicted, because I did not realize that I was. Once a friend of mine had pointed it out, I quit cold turkey. It was difficult to quit. Very painful, very sickening, but I pushed through it because I HATE the feeling of relying on something or someone. I strive to be self sufficient. And perhaps that stems from watching my mother do drugs, or the various bouts that my family has had with alcoholism, but regardless, I still display a HIGH threshold of resistance to substances. I've had drinks, and candy spiked like 4x throughout my life. 5 accounts of Food Poisoning, 1 account of Alcohol Poisoning. And even to this day, I consider myself to be "straight-edge."  Meaning; I don't drink or smoke anything. I just don't feel the effects as intensely as others do. And when I do feel intense reactions, my mind seems to override and negate those properties. I have personally found that I desperately seek out; "Balance."  Not just the physical sensation, but the discipline, the expression, even in financial wealth.  Deep down I know that struggling is actually good for you, because it builds strength and character. So I wonder if subconsciously, my mind strives to blend pain and pleasure into neutrality. That could offer an explanation as to why I feel so jaded. Why none of my life's accomplishments seem to matter to me very much.   All things that I'll have to consider next time I go to therapy.
