Author: @evelienheerens2879
Content:
There is some ableism here in this video.

I have been on medically prescribed fentanyl for almost a year, about two years ago, and have generally been on opoids for the better part of six years now.

I happen to have at least 7 distinct chronic pain disorders, I say at least is because once they found that many, they didnt feel like there was any use looking for others.

I take a dosage most doctors freak out about, but heres the kicker. I have never experienced euphoria from opoids. In fact, the maximum safe dosage barely takes the edge off of my pain.

Yes, after slowly increasing the dosage of fentanyl towards a pain level I could live with, I hit a ceiling where the side effects got dangerous, and going off cold turkey sucked.
But...

I had five boxes of patches lying on my table, and for the 2 weeks I was sweating, sleeping and throwing up and very little else, I was not once tempted to grab one. I simply went back on oxycodon after and was fine.

Addiction doesn't happen to everyone, and it doesn't affect everyone the same. Perhaps its because I never managed to get to the point of euphoria, I don't know. I do know that the amount of other pain killers I need to take to avoid going into shock if I don't take opoids, would be very very bad for me. For me they are life- saving drugs. Simply demonizing them this way is really really simplistic,

I wouldn't recommend anyone take them for kicks.But I also wouldnt recommend that for my adhd meds, or the steroids I take for my addisons. All drugs are garbage, they just also can happen te be something that keeps you alive or that keeps your quality of life from being garbage. Taking them if you don't need them is stupid, but so is not taking them if you do. Finding the right dosage and application and treatment plan is what doctors are for. Of course its great if a pharmaceutical company isnt allowed to incenticvise them to compromise on your care for their benefit, but I feel like society has swung around to blame the victims for the problems that caused.

long story short. I think this is a bad video. Without opoids, I wouldn't be alive today. If I lost access to them, I'd be dead in a year. And that wouldnt be a year Id wish on anyone.

I just wish this video wasn't steeped in the judgemental bullshit I have to deal with from care providers every time they see what meds I take. It's a list about 20 items long, but they always have to remark on the opioids. Pharmacies always have to make sure that you used up your very last dose before they give you a new one. I have landed in the emergency room a couple of time because of the consequences of a small supply chain hiccup, where the caution was that I would never have too many pills, rather than that I'd always have enough. After my doctor yelling at them for a few hours, a couple of angry letters and a few complaint procedures, that problem luckily doesn't occur anymore. But you can maybe imagine why I take issue with some of the sentiment in this video, as well as that some things stated as simple facts, that you will 100% get addicted and things like that. That it's a pure evil and an illegal drug which it isnt everywhere, and while it's controlled, so is adderal, so are cortico steroids and so are a whole bunch of other drugs you can just get access to with a prescription. It's just....not accurate. I expect better from you guys.

Content:
I have never used illicit drugs .. However I was given "Just a sniff of fentanyl in hospital" when I really didn't need it. The nurse asked how bad my chest pain was out of 10 (10 being the worst) and I replied 2.. she then insisted she gets me some fentanyl even though I initially refused... She said it will be "just a sniff". I Reckon she gave me some and kept the rest for her self..

But wow... As Someone that has chronic pain depression and anxiety I NEVER felt so good Best 20 or so minutes ever..  I have longed for a high like that ever since.

Fast forward to the last couple of weeks, I broke my hand, and my Dr gave me a 10 pack of Endone (Aussie Oxycodone) The only difference is the extended release. He prescribed 1x5mg pill twice daily..  I finished them in just over 2 days... Against my better judgement Taking 2 at a time.

I went back to the Dr for a check up and this time he gave me a 20 pack... That night I took 3 and experienced very little high...


In that moment I kinda scared my self and realized what I was doing.  I have the rest of the packet to my partner (who was a Family Drug Support worker) to dispose of.. 2 days on, the cravings are real!


I don't regret my decision to give my partner the pills, I wish there was a safe alternative to get the same high... 😢

Going forward I'm going to try and get medicinal marijuana....

Author: @bp968
Content:
This was actually poorly done, to my surprise.   It felt like a "DARE" ad from the 90s with a bit of science sprinkled in.

1) folks who want to take drugs recreationally are not effected by these style of ads/stories.  

2)  it did a poor job characterizing fentanyl.  Its actually an extremely useful drug, in the medical setting, for the same reason its a crappy recreational drug.  It's speed of action is extremely fast, and it wears off very quickly, making it excellent for medical procedures.  Its also excellent in pain patches because such a small amount of it is required to work for days on the patient, even patients with intestinal problems that preclude the use of other extended release medications.

I do think they covered *why* its a problem but failed to cover the cause of that problem.  Prohibition is the problem.  The more they crack down on illegal drugs the worse the problem gets.  It's human nature and will never go away, just like prostitution will never go away and making that illegal never works either.

Instead they should make (some) drugs legal and sell them through legit legal avenues.

This does four things:  1) it end (or severely reduces) the market for illegal drugs through violent and unregulated sources.  This is a huge benefit to everyone else out their that doesnt use or buy drugs.

2) it reduces the medical load, and societal costs because people won't need to hide it, will be more likely to keep safety medications on hand and have friends nearby to assist.  It will also reduce the ODs because the drugs will be carefully measured to exacting standards and not filled with garbage to improve a dealers profit.

3) it can be taxed, creating revenue to help deal with the problem. 

4) it will reduce the burden on legitimate users of legal medications (chronic pain patients, etc) and they will be more willing to be honest with their doctors because they wont fear the litany of legal repercussions if they were to make a mistake or foolish choice.

Unfortunately it will also have one additional effect and thats the reason it wont happen:  it will reduce the need for extreme enforcement, and will reduce the *massive* amount of money funneled into enforcement, prisons, and all the systems built and funded by the "war on drugs".  And it wont take you very long to find plenty of publicly available information about what a tremendous amount of money is involved and how many people it keeps employeed and agencies funded.

Author: @ArchTeryx00
Content:
I've had *medical* fentanyl quite a few times in my life, mostly because I need frequent procedures that require sedation. When they first inject it, you get a momentary high, then you start getting very woozy, and then...

That's one thing fentanyl, combined with the powerful benzodiazepine Versed, is extremely good at: Knocking you out cold. But it's not actual unconsciousness. It's a hypnotic state where you have no memory, no perception, no sense of time, *and no pain,* but can still follow basic instructions. 

Then about an hour or two later, you wake up in a recovery room. Procedure over, and you never felt or remember a thing.

The difference, however, is crucial. Under trained medical supervision, they can calculate exact doses and dilute fentanyl into saline to the dose required, with precision down to the nanogram. They have you on oxygen and effectively a BiPAP, to keep you breathing. They watch your heart rate VERY closely. If anything starts to go wrong, they have a crash team standing by ready to give you an antidote and/or ship you straight to the ER.


Fentanyl *in a medical setting* is a very low risk drug, and it can be amazing when used for its intended purpose: *Stopping pain.* But even here, they have to be very careful; they have to switch drugs if I am in the hospital too often, to prevent tolerance and addiction from occurring. And they will use less powerful opioids if they can, like Tramadol, which doesn't create as much of a high and lasts longer.

Fentanyl on the street, as Kurzgesagt says, is utterly lethal, because obviously none of the careful controls in a medical setting are in place. All it takes is a microgram too much, and your lungs or heart just quit.

Content:

Author: @gameplayer3050
Content:
This will most likely get lost but whatever.
When I was 16-17, I drank 2l of Cola per day. I kept up with this, because I also slept only 3 hours a day. I did this for ~4-6 months. During that time, a friend of my mother was diagnosed with diabetes Type II. I, being afraid that I might end like him (since he did the same thin I did only for much longer) quit drinking Cola and only drank water. I had such severe withdrawl symptoms that I could have died. The only way I could alleviate some of them (and literally stay alive) was to eat a toast with marmelade (aka a lot of sugar). The withdrawl symptoms kept up for 5 days and not relapsing to drinking cola/the massive amount of sugar was genuinely one of the hardest things I have ever done.....
1 year later, I was getting treated for depression. I took anti depressants in a very small dose. So small that, according to my doc, it was was basically just barely enough to have any effect on me. 
After I got better. (and especially so because the meds did not help at all) I just stopped taking them. 
Once again, I had withdrawl symptoms. This time, I persisted and did not take the medication. And I acted in ways I never would have done. 

If these are my symptoms from two "legal"/non extremely addictive substances, then I am genuinely afraid of how things would be if I ever took hard drugs. I am convinced that I would quite easily fall into the trap of addiction and not be able to climb out of it......

Author: @TemujinHead
Content: Addiction may be something out of one's control, but the first try DEFINITELY is a moral failing. If you aren't completely hooked, you can still make the decision to stop. Once it becomes a compulsion, it's out of your hands, but still on you for starting it. As for lacing, if it's lacing of another nonmedical drug (heroin, cocaine, weed), that's just an extra consequence of doing the first one. If it's lacing of medical drugs, not your fault the first time, but continuing is. If it's getting hooked on medical opioids, that's largely your doctor's fault for giving it to you (power through the pain, you wimp!/s), but you could always comply with the safety directives and not use them after you stop needing them. Drug addicts should be forgiven, but only after they commit to stopping.

Author: @laggingdragons
Content:
I was a straight edge kid until I was 19 but I always thought that the D.A.R.E. statement of "you can get addicted your first time using the drug" was just fear mongering. I found out they were right the first time I did cocaine. I love coke, and it is absolutely fucking horrifying because I know I shouldn't, and I wear it like a scar. I tell people the same thing every time so they understand that it's not worth trying.

Cocaine is a power star from Mario Bros. or a Quad Damage powerup from DOOM. You get this aura, it feels like you're wearing the spirit of a tiger, you have laser sharp focus and can enter flow on anything with just a thought. It literally makes you feel like Wolverine, like the alcohol doesn't hit, like you could win any fight, accomplish any goal.

For 30 minutes.

Then you're back to normal. In your body you feel self-conscious about, with your regular, every day reaction times and tolerance. Your head is filled with doubt again instead of focus, and your body moves in slow motion as everything blurs instead of feeling crystal clear like it did. You're just another human being again, and you feel small, inadequate, and kind of scared.

I've kind of always wanted to try opium, for the same reason I tried cocaine, but I know not to listen. Same reason I won't touch datura or what have you: I have found that there are some things we are not meant to know. Life is precious, don't try to escape yours, own it instead. Strength comes from practice, not distraction; macguffins are not real.

Author: @NoobixCube
Content:
I'm disappointed to have never experienced a high from any opioid. I've had various ones used on me during medical procedures. It takes about double the dose they want to give me to shut any kind of pain out, and I can _still feel it,_ and I get no floating sensation like people describe. I get no positive feeling from opioids at all. It was to the point after my most recent surgery, I just wasn't using the patient controlled analgesia button. The does was set at normal human levels, I didn't get any effect from it, and it just made me constipated. Because I wasn't self-administering, the nurses started feeding me endone pills which I said to them were doing nothing but giving me abdominal pain from the constipation, but they kept feeding me the pills. Any time someone says the pain pills aren't enough or aren't doing anything, nurses just ignore that, because that's what a junkie after a fix would be saying.

As I was going in for that surgery, when they were going to put me out with a dose of methadone first (I'd had negative reactions to general anaesthetic in the past, so they wanted to sedate me so they could use less GA), I warned them that I suspect I'm insensitive to opioids. I got a "yep, ahuh", from the nurse, and saw the familiar look from her that said "he's just after a bigger fix". She gave me a shot of methadone, kept me talking and kept tracking my attention to gauge the effect. A few minutes later she frowned a bit, gave me another dose, and kept me talking. I kept on being alert and responsive and she eventually just said "HOW ARE YOU STILL UPRIGHT?!". I just said "I warned you, opioid insensitive. All I've got is a bit of trouble keeping my eyes fixed vertically, everything seems to be rolling down on me." I think she must have given me enough methadone to put down a cow.

For a biopsy on my kidney, prior to this surgery, they used fentanyl to sedate me because the needed me awake, but getting stabbed in the kidney is one of the most painful things it's possible to experience. At this point, I had no idea how severe my insensitivity was. I knew codeine did nothing for me but I figured fentanyl would do the job. They gave me the usual dose, and tested my sensation with sharp pokes in various locations and asking me if I felt them (and I assume no pokes and asking if I felt those, to check I wasn't just saying yes). They obviously determined I could still feel too much for their liking, gave me another hit, and it crashed my blood pressure hard because I'd been fasting for the procedure. They stabilised that somehow, then repeated the sensation tests. I could still feel everything but it was a little dulled. I just had to say to them, "I'm a little numb now, but I don't think you can give me more fentanyl without something bad happening. Just go ahead, I'll deal with it". I was numb enough that I kept the screams on the inside, but it still really fucking hurt.

Doctors, nurses, whatever, if you're reading this, and you later hear a patient say opioids don't do it for them, obviously _consider_ drug-seeking behaviour, but please believe your patients. Opioid insensitivity is a real thing.

Content:
Fentanyl is primarily for ICU use, especially when administered as a continuous infusion. I was on iv fentanyl for 11 weeks. Being 24/7 on invasive ventilation. The fentanyl was combined with morphine. Here is why.
Fentanyl for Dyspnea Management in Invasively Ventilated Patients
Indication: Fentanyl is used exclusively in ICU settings as part of sedation and analgesia protocols in mechanically ventilated patients, particularly to reduce dyspnea (the sensation of breathlessness) and improve patient–ventilator synchrony.
Mechanism of Action:
Fentanyl is a potent synthetic opioid that:
- Reduces central perception of dyspnea via µ-opioid receptor activation.
- Provides analgesia without significant histamine release (unlike morphine).
- Has a rapid onset and short duration, making it suitable for continuous IV infusion.
Clinical Benefits:
- Reduces the sensation of air hunger in ventilated patients.
- Helps with ventilator synchrony and reduces agitation.
- May lower the need for deep sedation or paralytics.
It helped me a lot.

– **Surgery**: Maintains stable vital signs during high-risk procedures,  
– **Cancer Palliative Care**: Transdermal patches provide 72-hour pain relief for terminal patients,

**The crisis stems from illicit analogs** (85% of U.S. overdose deaths!), not regulated medical use. In Canada, **1.2 million patients** receive fentanyl safely annually under strict protocols. Let’s combat misinformation: demonizing a vital drug hinders both patient care and scientific progress.

Author: @rustyshackleford6927
Content:
Hey, actual (mostly recovered) junkie here. The whole “the first is the best & you’ll never feel that same bliss again” is bullshit. The first time is usually trash. Yeah you get an initial flood of bliss & pain relief, but most first timers then start puking their guts out from nausea, which dampens the “fun” bits of being high af. & if one keeps their doses low, & spaced out long enough for it’s half-life of efficacy in your system, they can relive the same level of feel-good high as the first initial dope-rush. It’s only when you get greedy & start chasing that feeling by doing more too soon that leads to not being able to relive that moment again.

Also, the “one hit & you’re hooked” is also bullshit. Though it depends on your brain chemistry & life circumstances, it’s habitual use, leading to physical dependence that causes problems. Personally, I used dope for a couple years before becoming physically dependant… because I started using more than 2x/week when I was in an abusive situation, became homeless, & then suffered an injury that needed intense pain relief for an extended period.

Most drug users are totally normal people whom you’d never even guess were using/hooked… unfortunately it’s the extreme cases on the street that people see that overshadows the rest of us.

Drug use is is a normal human activity. Almost everyone has used drugs in some capacity in their lives… hell, how many people can’t function without their morning coffee? That headache one gets when they haven’t had their morning cup is WITHDRAWAL because the body is addicted!! But it’s legal, so no one bats an eye about it. With illicit drugs, the biggest harms come from prohibition itself, because illicit markets are unregulated, making the substances quality a crapshoot.

Fent is a direct symptom of prohibition, & capitalism. Were heroin/milder opioids legally accessible to those that need it, & proper healthcare, harm reduction, & addiction services available (& not heavily stigmatized) fent wouldn’t have become as huge as it currently is. But since fent is so potent, it’s easier to smuggle in more of it in smaller, more easy to conceal packages, so dealers chose to reduce their risk by swapping heroin for fent. Especially bc they could cut it down with inert powders or baby laxatives to get more sales out of the smaller amount, while still providing similar effects (plus, fent has a much shorter half life than heroin, making users needs more, more often, which also increased dealer profits)

I could go on for hours about this subject… I worked in public health doing harm reduction outreach for years so have academic- as well as first hand—knowledge of the subject. But I’ll stop here. Though if anyone has questions I’d be happy to answer whatever I can if anyone replies to this (if it doesn’t get deleted that is…😅)

Content:
I’m addicted to Fentanyl now. Have been for years. These kinds of videos are hard to watch. When it comes down to it, some days it easier to pretend everything is normal even when it isn’t. Author: @emmareiman64
Content:
The descriptions of the withdrawals
My brain: "Ooooh, so whatever we're feeling whenever our anxieties flare up" aka, a period of 3+ months straight I had at the end of last year. It was Hell.
I've never taken drugs, never been tempted to nor have I ever even considered them

Still won't try stuff though, if ever in doubt, I'll just think of the times where I've naturally experienced such highs - like petting our or anyone else's dogs, having a nice little chat or joking about with friends, or whenever I've been able to help out anyone (be that via completing chores as a group, listing things super clearly to make something easier for others, or helping to mentally reassure someone - it's all really good to me)
There are times that are garbage, but there's also plenty of small good little things - like making it on the bus in time, trying out new foods or berries that you end up really enjoying, etc etc. No matter how small, natural joys hit the hardest and beat out any drugs to me

Author: @ReversingDiabetes
Content:
I have never experienced what you're describing in spite of two long-term rounds of opioid use.  

After my bypass, when I got out of the hospital where I'd been on morphine, I was prescribed percocet.  It annoyingly made me high while I couldn't physically do anything and was stuck in bed.  They switched me to a fentanyl patch so I could read to entertain myself.  I rarely took perc for breakthrough pain, the patch mostly controlled it.  I was on-and-off that stuff for a few months until I didn't need it anymore.

A decade later, a large portion of my leg was surgically removed.  The wound was such that the muscles had to be pushed back in at every dressing change!  I was on oxycodone for pain generally, but it was especially necessary for me during physical therapy and occupational therapy as I learned to stand and walk again. As I had less pain, I took less meds, until I was off them entirely after about a year.  It's been around 7 years now since I needed any.

Neither of my experiences was anything like the heaven you describe.  I did feel a bit stoned at first, but that went away rapidly.  Within a week, I felt perfectly normal on opioids, not stoned in the least.  I never increased dosage, in fact the opposite, I decreased as the pain subsided.  And I never had anything like withdrawal, I just used them less as I needed them less until I didn't need them any more.

I had a doctor once say that I didn't have a problem because I don't have an addictive personality.  But I come from a family of addicts, so whether it's genetic or environmental, I should have addiction problems.  And I do - I had 50 years of nicotine addiction and likely most would identify me as a caffeine addict to this day.  

It just never seemed to me, nor others I know dealing with actual long-term pain, anything like what you describe.  I mean, having some heavenly experience sounds kinda fun, but that never happened.  The "stoned" I felt at first wasn't even as intense as alcohol or pot (neither of which I've done for years either).

I don't know anything about recreational use of them except I had a home health aid who swiped some of them once, which irritated me as I needed them!  

But I wouldn't recommend them for recreational use mostly just because IME they weren't particularly fun.   

I don't do anything recreationally, unless you count caffeine, and haven't for many years.  I do regularly receive oxytocin because I have a very cuddly kitty.  ;)

I don't doubt some addicts have described the experience you describe, just there is apparently another way to experience opioids that is totally different.

Author: @GigaLigma
Content:
Never have I had a drug psa try to convince me not to try a drug by trying to convince me to try a different better drug instead.

Also, the message here is basically that "drugs open your eyes to how horrible life really is." It's sad and maybe a bit counterproductive as a message, but it's true, that's where the addiction comes from. It's not like your body is literally forcing you (although when you become extremely addicted obviously you have extreme physical withdrawal, but a person is usually mentally dependent long before and after then), you just don't want to experience normal life anymore after having something else to compare it to and that's the real fuel to addiction. That's what gets people relapsing months or years after they've overcome the physical part of addiction: no matter how long they try to resist it, they're forever burdened with the understanding of how terrible life really is and how much better they could feel if their mind would only let them.

It's sad to think that the real source of addiction is just enlightenment. Asking people to avoid addictive substances is literally just asking them to avoid experiencing pleasure they can't imagine, because they won't ever be able to look at life without it the same way again. We just aren't meant to be truly happy.

Author: @kylinsky
Content: The purpose of fentanyl is to be administered to people suffering from a terminal illness such as cancer, who have severe pain and difficulty swallowing; the drug is typically given through a transdermal patch that gives extremely small does over a 72 hours period. Its dose is so small that it is measured in micrograms per hour; so, a person taking even 1mg in a single dose is taking a dose massively greater than it was ever intended to be used in a clinical setting over a 3-day period, and of course it was never intended for a recreational use. I don't have any solutions for the crisis, but it would be a terrible shame if the fentanyl black market were to cost us a long-proven pain management option for hospice patients.

So, essentially, the Fentanyl crisis is just another of our own making. We criminalize drugs to the point that dealers commoditize worse hybrid drugs with extremely addictive substances laced in, we blame the individuals more than those dealers or our own inept government despite those individuals lacking the facilities to overcome such an addiction (one which the rest of us cannot begin to comprehend the struggle of), and we sit around with our thumbs up our butts looking at statistics and listening to inept (and typically, right aligning) politicians who think further authoritarianism is the solution.

You cannot fix the addicts without care facilities or at the very least a clean supply with prescriptive controls to wean them off their substance gradually, the typical American will not experience an addiction of this magnitude in their entire lives so they lack the scope to understand its toll. You can fix the legislation surrounding drugs and (by extension) help regulate the supply that addicts are putting into their bodies, so the way forward is obvious to anyone with any brain activity whatsoever. 

A question for the simpletons who actually advocate for harsh drug control: When's the last time forcibly restricting someone from doing something resulted in total compliance? Ashley Madison had 73 percent of users identifying as Christian aligning despite them being explicitly told (in a commandment, I think) that such activity is forbidden. Humans are innately rebellious, forcible compliance is a game of attrition and is entirely to blame for the current state of America.

Author: @scottkidder9046
Content:
Drugs seem impossible to deal with, all you can do is manage it. I’m at the point now where I’m ready to support legalizing many of these drugs for medical use in the sense that if you’ve been diagnosed with an addiction, you can get safe doses of these hard drugs and perhaps eventually wean your way off them. I’m even willing to have places where people can go to get doses without fentanyl and take it supervised. I’m all for trying to stop drugs at the border, but we aren’t going to get anywhere if it’s laced into every other drug that has a high demand. We have to make regulated hard drugs competitive and cheap. At least then people won’t OD and we’ll have a better idea of the state of our drug crisis at any given time. It sounds crazy, but 80,000 unsuspecting mostly young kids dying a year is enough to make me do pretty much anything to try and stop it. Policing it isn’t the solution because most victims aren’t trying to use fentanyl. 

Also, please don’t be afraid of fentanyl when it’s used in a hospital setting or with a prescription. It’s used all the time for post surgical pain and for pain management for those with severe chronic pain. It’s not ideal in the chronic case obviously, but it’s the best we have in many cases. You can try other methods and if they take away your pain, thank God. But if it persists, there’s no shame in using it to help manage things. The scourge of fentanyl has nothing to do it being used in hospitals. There are horror stories, but they’re exceptions, not rules, and they don’t explain why young people are dying in such huge numbers. The crisis is because it’s laced with other hard drugs on the street and people don’t realize they’re taking it, not that people are getting it for post surgical pain. The fentanyl in a hospital is extremely tightly regulated. 

Honestly, if you know you’re likely to take drugs, there are kits that you can use to quickly tell if what you’re taking has fentanyl in it. Take 2 minutes and test what you’re taking before doing it. It’s lame, but it could very well save your life. Also, it’s better to do them with other people. Have narcan with you no matter what drug you’re doing. Even if there’s one person who has narcan in the group, they can reverse the drug’s effects if they realize you’ve OD’d

Content: Hey, before you even think about trying opioids, stop and truly imagine what you’re facing—it’s like staring into a dark, bottomless abyss. That first leap might feel like a free fall, making you feel alive, tingling, and free, but that rush is a lie that fades into nothing, leaving you empty. Opioids hijack your brain’s reward system, flooding dopamine receptors with artificial highs until the hobbies or art you love—painting, music, or whatever brings you joy—feel dull and lifeless. The bursts of euphoria you once got from those passions vanish because heavy opioid use overstimulates your brain, numbing it to natural pleasures. The deeper you fall, the more you’ll need just to feel “okay,” while the things that made you *you* become meaningless. Addiction is a trap—most jump in, but few crawl out, forever changed. Instead, chase something real and meaningful. A hobby or skill might be hit-or-miss at first, but the more you invest, the more progress and joy you create—unlike opioids, which demand more and give less. Opioids are an empty promise that’ll steal everything you love. Think hard about that one thing that lights you up—don’t let drugs take it away.

Author: @Leyrann
Content:
I get prescribed some (milder) opioids for my ADHD, and recently we switched to a different variation, which meant having to test what the right dose would be. So, with a very quick feedback loop with the doctor of course, I've been taking gradually higher doses until the negative effects became clear. With my previous medication, those negative effects were simply that the medication started doing the opposite of what it was supposed to - making my brain more hyperactive instead of less, which was annoying for a few days but that was that. However, with this new medication, during the day things went perfectly fine, but during the night I'd start having heart palpitations, generally feeling bad, some slight twitching at times, stuff like that. It was like my very own, very minor taste of withdrawal and I absolutely hated it. Luckily I did have some of the lower dose medication still lying around, so I could switch back to that immediately, without even having to contact the doctor prescribing it.

I suppose the good thing that came out of it is that I have some minor empirical support for the suspicion that I wouldn't be prone to indulge in a drug again to stave off the withdrawal, because if anything, I wanted to stay AWAY from the higher dosage based on how it made me feel when it WASN'T active. That was a far bigger and more obvious negative to me than the improvement during the day (when it was active) was a positive. Which, now that I think about it, might be in part because of the gradual increase in dosage (while obviously sitting at levels for medical use, rather than "flood the entire system in happiness hormones!"), which made the improvement appear more minor in the first place as I wasn't actually comparing to how I felt _completely_ without.

Content:
I can imagine it's because artificially enhanced heroine. - as a currently regular user of opioids, and by that i mean using dihydrocodeine 2 to 3 times a week, i can confidently say i have no physical tolerance or very little so its always fun and doesn't require me to take higher doses, no or very little withdrawal syndrome (tested it through pauses when i decide to stop using for weeks/months without any problems), no social problems, i have a stable job and life, no mental health issues, no health problems (i go to the gym and eat healthy)

Author: @y_fam_goeglyd
Content:
If you're on opioids for physical reasons (i.e. disabilities, constant pain - real, genuine physical pain that traps you in bed all day), you won't have a clue about the so-called joys of taking them. I'm on quite a lot of pain meds, including an opioid, and I've not once been "high". Never so much as not been in some level of pain in over 40 years (on some form of opiate for about 10 years). My mildest days would have most people calling an ambulance. 

So thanks for this, because I've never understood the desire to take any sort of drug, and never understood how those I take under supervision are supposed to be addictive and "fun". I can forget to take my opiate - I write down when I take anything, and doing it first can leave me thinking I've taken them. I don't often notice, I just think that they're not working, because there are days when they don't. I don't get any negative side effects, no withdrawal or anything like that. Doc thinks I'm essentially "immune" to them. They're probably right after all this time!

I see that there are people here who have suffered as a result of fentanyl. I am so sorry for your suffering, whether it's as a direct result of taking it or because you lost someone you loved 😢. Drug dealers are simply the scum of the earth. 🤬

Content:
Okay, this makes sense now why the USA is so crazy about stopping this drug from coming in. Until I watched this I was completely lost when politicians mentioned it, I mean I knew it was some form of drug, but I’d never heard of it before, the drugs I’m more familiar with are Heroin, Cocaine, Cannabis and Weed, and only by reputation not personal.

Hearing that breakdown, yea, makes sense why Dealers like this drug so much, cheap easy money, and they don’t really care about their customers, I hate saying this and I’m aware it may offend some people, but this is a market where I don’t think the demand will ever fully disappear without action being taken, if you know what I mean. So yea, they’re gonna keep making that S*** and cutting it with other drugs.

The only way I can see the market being dismantled for good, is educating the younger generations about this stuff and how dangerous it is. The problem is so many people will say, ignorance is bliss, don’t educate as that might encourage them to seek it out. In my opinion, that’s just dumb, especially given what you said about dealers secretly adding Fentanyl to other drugs to make them more addictive. If people don’t know, they can’t make an informed decision, educate and educate the right way, that’s the only defence against the bastards who make this stuff.

And no I don’t want anyone to say anything about the Mexicans or Canadians smuggling over the border. Even if it IS true (and actual facts say most Fentanyl is manufactured INSIDE the US), the smuggling only occurs because there’s a market, there’s money to be made. You don’t destroy a market by cutting off its supply, because criminals will ALWAYS find a way to get that supply… you destroy a market by going after the Demand.

Prime example, Rhino Horn.

Many have said that in order to stop Poaching of White Rhinos for their Horns, you need to Ban the Trade of Rhino Horn (attacking the supply). This is a stupid idea however, because the problem is again, the Demand, so long as the Demand exists, criminals will find a way to supply that Demand, ESPECIALLY if it’s illegal, cause now they can make customers pay through the NOSE for it, because they can’t get it anywhere else. The better method is to make it more difficult to sell illegally obtained Rhino Horn, forcing poachers to drive up their prices, while making it easier to sell legally obtained Rhino horn (for those who don’t know, so long as the animal is alive, the horn WILL grow back, so while it raises ethical questions, many wildlife parks will safely dehorn Rhinos to protect them from poachers, then sell the horn to make a profit), which is then cheaper and doesn’t come with the legal ramifications of possessing illegal Rhino Horn, making it more appealing to buyers, while simultaneously giving the animals value to those who protect them, which provides incentive to do so.

The only problem is, last I checked, the folks who govern this sort of stuff are dragging their feet on regulating this whole issue, but once they do, and we see demand for illegal Rhino horn drop, while demand for legal Rhino Horn rises, the poachers will be out of business.

Content: You should mention Narcan. It is an OTC medication that quickly reverses the effects of an opioid overdose (including fentanyl) by blocking opioid receptors (if given in time). For people who take drugs, take them with someone who can safely monitor you and administer it and call for emergency services if need be. You can also buy fentanyl test strips to test the drugs you are taking for $1-2 each. Test strips are not 100% accurate, depending on conditons and the drug concoction, so still use caution. Unfortunately, taking street drugs is still a reality, even in this fentanyl-laced world, so try to mitigate harm where you can.

Author: @garayur
Content: Harm Reductionist here, while there is good information in this video, it also has a lot of harmful terminology and unintentional misinformation. Stigma is a huge factor in drug harm and as such we try to be careful with our language. For example we use substance use, physical dependency, and disordered use instead of addict or addiction. Additionally the rise of fentanyl is the direct consequence of the increased criminalization of heroine. There is also no evidence that fentanyl is mixed in with other drugs intentionally. There is also no mention of how street opioids are often used due to the lack of access to the medical system. Nitazenes are also entering the street supply, which can be significantly stronger than fentanyl.

Author: @worsel555
Content:
Oh boy, I have a feeling this is going to be another video about fentanyl that is going to drive me up the wall due to people not really fully understanding it and thus treat it like the boogeyman, or try to demonize everyone who uses it like we are a bunch of addicts.  I am on fentanyl and I also take dilaudid (around 10x stronger than morphine) twice a day on top of it, and it is just barely enough to let me function and go to work.

Unfortunately, I am one of those truly rare individuals who is opioid resistant so most things that would be super strong or outright cause someone to overdose will not affect me at all. Some of you out there reading this may think "Wow, that's awesome!" and let me tell you that no, it is not.  I am condemned to a lifetime of needless pain.  Ever have dental work done without novocaine?  I have had four shots and it does absolutely nothing, so I just tell the dentist to work quickly.  How about going in for surgery and your Anesthetist has not bothered to read your chart in full and ignored the large, repeated warnings saying that you are opioid resistant and that you will require 4x what would kill someone just to put you out?  Cant tell you how many times I have been wheeled into an operating room and everyone involved is semi freaking out that I am still wide awake, alert, and asking if they want me to help them out before they start throwing everything they have to get me under.

I have major joint and disk issues which has resulted in several fusions, in fact I am waiting for my next one sometime this fall, but it's frustrating to see so many people not understand how useful this medication can be as it is the only thing in a world of endless suffering that can make it somewhat tolerable, but that is for me and if it was for someone else I am sure they would be looking for a way to make it stop forever, and I am not going to lie, that was considered once before I was put on fentanyl.

Don't let the actions of some people demonize what has been a literal life saving medication for myself and others, and don't believe those videos where a cop touches it and suddenly falls over with a vacant stare, that's not how this works and you can swim in a pool of the stuff and it wont get you high.  It's actually VERY hard to get it to pass through the skin, and even harder to inhale.  You don't have to take my word for it, ask an Anesthetist the next time you're in a hospital and they will tell you the same thing.

Just expect to also get some weird follow-up questions :)  I also recommend Skip Intro's video "What Cop Shows get WRONG about FENTANYL" as it is very well researched and backed up with actual studies and sources, so go watch that AFTER this video.

Now if you will excuse me, and if anyone actually read my rant before even I watched this video myself, thank you. It's not easy to see stuff like this and very few people even know I am on it.
